bib.title: Latent Retrieval for Weakly Supervised Open Domain Question Answering

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Latent Retrieval for Weakly Supervised Open Domain Question Answering", Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Kristina Toutanova (Google Research). ACL 2019, Proceedings pages 6086–6096. The file is the ACL proceedings version, not the arXiv 1906.00300 preprint layout.

COVERAGE: I read all 43,726 of 43,726 chars: the body, Tables 1–7, all three figure captions and the references. The paper has no appendix. Page numbers below are PDF pages. p1 is proceedings page 6086, so PDF page = proceedings page − 6085.

CLAIMS
- claim: ORQA trains a retriever and reader together using only question-answer string pairs, with no IR system. The authors say they are the first to do this. Retrieval over all of Wikipedia is treated as a latent variable.
  number: none
  setup: English Wikipedia (Dec 20, 2018 snapshot), over 13M blocks; BERT-base encoders
  quote: "We show for the ﬁrst time that it is possible to jointly learn the retriever and reader from question-answer string pairs and without any IR system. In this setting, evidence retrieval from all of Wikipedia is treated as a latent variable."
  where: p1, abstract
- claim: On datasets where the person writing the question did not know the answer, learned retrieval beats BM25 by 6 to 19 EM points.
  number: Test EM, ORQA vs BM25+BERT: Natural Questions 33.3 vs 26.5; WebQuestions 36.4 vs 17.7; CuratedTrec 30.1 vs 21.3. Dev: NQ 31.3 vs 24.8; WQ 38.5 vs 20.8; CT 36.8 vs 27.1.
  setup: Table 5, end-to-end exact match. Both systems use the same BERT reader and only QA pairs. BM25 retrieval is static during fine-tuning, and its final score is a learned weighted sum of BM25 and reader scores. ORQA retrieves top k=5.
  quote: "our ICT pre-trained retriever outperforms BM25 by a large marge—6 to 19 points in exact match depending on the dataset." (the typo "marge" is in the source)
  where: p8 (Table 5 on p7)
- claim: On datasets where the question writer already knew the answer (SQuAD, TriviaQA), BM25 matches or beats ORQA. The authors' explanation is that a compressed 128-dimensional vector cannot represent every word the way BM25 does.
  number: Test EM: TriviaQA BM25 47.1 vs ORQA 45.0; SQuAD 33.2 vs 20.2. Dev: TriviaQA 47.2 vs 45.1; SQuAD 28.1 vs 26.5.
  setup: Table 5, same conditions as above
  quote: "in datasets where the question askers already know the answer, i.e. SQuAD and TriviaQA, the retrieval problem resembles traditional IR. In this setting, a highly compressed 128-dimensional vector cannot match BM25's ability to precisely represent every word in the evidence."
  where: p8
- claim: The question-writing bias argument. Questions written by someone who already knows the answer are not driven by a need for information, so they contain hints. SQuAD writers also saw the evidence passage, which creates artificial word overlap between question and evidence. The information-seeking datasets (NQ, WQ, CuratedTrec) have a different, "moderate" bias: annotators find answers with tools.
  number: none
  setup: Section 7.2 and Table 4, a qualitative breakdown of the five datasets
  quote: "Question writing is not motivated by an information need. This often results in many hints in the question that would not be present in naturally occurring questions ... This is particularly problematic for SQuAD, where the question askers are also prompted with a speciﬁc piece of evidence for the answer, leading to artiﬁcially large lexical overlap between the question and evidence."
  where: p6
- claim: The large drop from dev to test on SQuAD comes from the dataset itself, because its questions come from very few documents. The authors advise against using SQuAD to train or evaluate learned open-domain retrieval.
  number: 100k questions from 536 documents
  setup: open SQuAD, Table 5 (ORQA dev 26.5 vs test 20.2)
  quote: "its 100k questions are derived from only 536 documents. Therefore, good retrieval targets are highly correlated between training examples, violating the IID assumption, and making it unsuitable for learned retrieval."
  where: p8
- claim: The Inverse Cloze Task (ICT) pretrains the retriever. A random sentence acts as a pseudo-question and the text around it acts as pseudo-evidence. The model must pick the true context from the other blocks in the batch, which serve as negatives (softmax over in-batch candidates).
  number: none
  setup: Section 4; Wikipedia blocks
  quote: "In ICT, a sentence is treated as a pseudo-question, and its context is treated as pseudo-evidence. Given a pseudo-question, ICT requires selecting the corresponding pseudo-evidence out of the candidates in a batch."
  where: p2
- claim: The sentence is removed from its context only 90% of the time. Masking 100% of the time costs almost 10 EM points because the model never learns to use word overlap. Masking 0% of the time costs about 6 points and performs about the same as BM25.
  number: 90% masking rate; about −10 EM (always mask), −6 EM (never mask)
  setup: Fig. 3, Natural Questions open dev set
  quote: "If we always mask the pseudo-query, the retriever never learns that n-gram overlap is a powerful retrieval signal, losing almost 10 points in end-to-end performance. If we never mask the pseudo-query ... The latter loses 6 points in end-to-end performance, which—perhaps not surprisingly—produces near-identical results to BM25."
  where: p8
- claim: Because of ICT, the block encoder can stay frozen after pretraining. All blocks are encoded once into an index for maximum inner product search, and only the question encoder and reader are fine-tuned.
  number: none
  setup: Sections 4–6
  quote: "We can expect the block encoder BERT B(b) to work well without further training. Only the question encoder needs to be ﬁne-tuned on downstream data."
  where: p5
- claim: Without ICT almost no training example would have the answer in its retrieved blocks. With ICT, fewer than 10% of examples are discarded.
  number: <10% discarded
  setup: fine-tuning with full-loss top-k=5 and early-update c=5000
  quote: "While we would expect almost all examples to be discarded with random initialization, we discard less than 10% of examples in practice due to ICT pre-training."
  where: p5
- claim: Unsupervised language-model embeddings do very poorly as retrievers. This shows that being pretrained as a language model is not the same as being trained for retrieval.
  number: NQ test EM: NNLM 4.0, ELMo 4.7 (vs BM25 26.5, ORQA 33.3)
  setup: Table 5. The LM encoders are 128-dimensional and pre-encode the blocks; the question encoder is fine-tuned.
  quote: "Natural Questions 26.5 4.0 4.7 33.3" (Table 5 test row; columns BM25+BERT, NNLM+BERT, ELMo+BERT, ORQA)
  where: p7
- claim: The BM25 baseline is strong. In the strongly supervised DrQA setting with 5 blocks, it beats 5-document BERTserini and comes close to 29-paragraph BERTserini.
  number: SQuAD EM 34.7 (BM25+BERT, 5 blocks) vs BERTserini 19.1 (5 docs), 36.6 (29 paragraphs), 38.6 (100 paragraphs); DrQA 27.1–29.8
  setup: Table 6. Reader pretrained on SQuAD gold derivations; Dec 12, 2016 Wikipedia snapshot.
  quote: "our BM25 baseline, which retrieves 5 evidence blocks, greatly outperforms 5-document BERTserini and is close to 29-paragraph BERTserini."
  where: p8
- claim: Implementation scale: about 13M blocks of at most 288 wordpieces; BERT-base uncased; 128-dimensional retrieval vectors so the system fits on one machine; ICT run for 100k steps at batch size 4096 on TPUs; fine-tuning at batch size 1 on a 12GB GPU.
  number: 288 wordpieces; 13M blocks; 128-dim; batch 4096; 100k steps
  quote: "When pre-training the retriever with ICT, we use a learning rate of10−4 and a batch size of 4096 on Google Cloud TPUs for 100k steps."
  where: p6–7

LIMITS
- The 128-dimensional dense vectors represent very specific concepts poorly. Sparse methods separate these cleanly. The authors point to hybrid dense-plus-sparse retrieval as future work: "ORQA has trouble precisely representing extremely speciﬁc concepts that sparse representations can cleanly separate. These errors indicate that a hybrid approach would be promising future work." (p9)
- ORQA does not beat BM25 on TriviaQA or SQuAD.
- The paper reports no retrieval-only metrics such as recall@k. Every number is end-to-end exact match, so retriever and reader effects cannot be separated.
- There are no confidence intervals or seeds; each result is a single number. The masking ablation is reported on NQ dev only.
- The authors concede that every dataset has some bias, and say this is a property of the data rather than a criticism of how it was collected: "it is unclear how one could collect a truly unbiased dataset without impractical costs." (p6)
- Dated: the reader is extractive (spans of at most 10 tokens), not generative. Later work superseded this, and the paper itself does not report that.
- The corpus is a Dec 2018 snapshot, not DrQA's 2016 corpus, so Table 5 cannot be compared directly with earlier work. Table 6 uses the 2016 snapshot for that reason.

BUILDS ON
- BERT (Devlin et al., 2018): all encoders.
- Cloze task (Taylor, 1953): ICT is its inverse.
- ICT described as "a generalization of the skip-gram objective (Mikolov et al., 2013)" with "in-batch negative sampling from Logeswaran and Lee (2018)".
- DrQA (Chen et al., 2017): open-QA setup, TF-IDF pipeline, evaluation script.
- Weak supervision from TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), SearchQA (Dunn et al., 2017), Quasar (Dhingra et al., 2017).
- BM25 (Robertson et al., 2009) and BERTserini (Yang et al., 2019) as baselines. Lin (2019) is cited on the difficulty of beating weak IR baselines.
- Span representation from Lee et al. (2016).
- "QA is fundamentally different from IR (Singh, 2012)".
- Weakly supervised semantic parsing (Clarke et al., 2010; Liang et al., 2013; Berant et al., 2013).

CODE: none. The paper has only equations. The ones worth keeping, as written: retrieval score "Sretr(b, q) = h⊤q hb" (p3); ICT objective "PICT (b|q) = exp(Sretr(b, q))∑ b′∈BATCH exp(Sretr(b′, q))" (p4); final loss "L(q, a) = Learly(q, a) + Lfull(q, a)" (p5).

FIGURES
- Figure 2, p4: "Example of the Inverse Cloze Task (ICT), used for retrieval pre-training. A random sentence (pseudo-query) and its context (pseudo evidence text) are derived from the text snippet ... The objective is to select the true context among candidates in the batch." This is the best candidate. The zebra example shows a pseudo-query that never mentions "zebra" being matched to its context, which explains in-batch-negative self-supervision faster than prose can.
- Figure 1, p3: an overview of ORQA that shows the retriever and reader working as two stages. It fits the "two components" section of note 02.
- Figure 3, p8: a plot of NQ dev EM against ICT masking rate, with a horizontal BM25 line. It is a good illustration of the trade-off between word overlap and semantic matching.

PROBLEMS
- Table 4 lost its checkmarks in extraction. The text shows dataset names under the column headers but no marks, so I cannot read from the table which bias applies to which dataset. Section 7.2's prose gives the mapping: NQ, WQ and CuratedTrec have tool-assisted answers; TriviaQA and SQuAD writers know the answer; SQuAD writers also know the evidence.
- Some table text is run together, e.g. the Table 6 header "Evidence SQuADRetrieved" and "34.7(gold deriv.)".
- The "6 to 19" range is the authors' rounding. The exact test gaps are 6.8, 18.7 and 8.8; the dev gaps are 6.5, 17.7 and 9.7.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
